bottle.still: Distilled twice at Carbost in five copper pot stills, two for the wash and three for the spirit, a layout kept from the days of triple distillation. U-shaped lyne arms on the wash stills send some vapour back, and wooden worm tubs outside condense the rest.

records.table: Talisker 10 Year Old is a single malt from Skye, made at Carbost on the shore of Loch Harport since 1830: sea spray and smoke first, then dried fruit and a burst of black pepper. Pour it neat with a little water beside it.
records.story: In 1830 two brothers who had come to Skye from the Isle of Eigg, the MacAskills, founded a distillery at Carbost, on the shore of Loch Harport, with a lease from the MacLeods. Robert Louis Stevenson (1850 to 1894) named it in 1880, in his poem The Scotsman's Return from Abroad, as one of the king of drinks beside Islay and Glenlivet. The distillery passed to the Distillers Company in 1925, and in 1928 it gave up triple distillation for double, though it kept its three spirit stills beside the two for the wash. In November 1960 a fire burned down the house where the stills stood, and the stills were rebuilt as exact copies of the old ones so that the spirit would not change; the old worm tubs outside were spared. The distillery's own maltings closed in 1972. At the end of the 1980s the 10 Year Old was chosen as one of the Classic Malts, the island malt of the set. For a bartender it is the bottle that shows a guest what a maritime Scotch means: salt, smoke and pepper in one glass.

others.name: Talisker Distillers Edition
others.note: A second maturation in casks seasoned with Amoroso sherry, bottled by vintage at 45.8% ABV.

traps: Talisker is an island malt, but in law it is a Highland single malt: the Scotch Whisky Regulations protect no Islands region, only Islay and Campbeltown as localities.
Talisker is made on Skye, not on Islay: it is often poured beside Islay malts for its smoke, but its home is Carbost on Loch Harport.

bottle.name: Highland Park 12 Year Old Viking Honour Single Malt Scotch Whisky
bottle.class: Single malt Scotch whisky; an island malt from Orkney, Highland in law
bottle.mash: Malted barley only. About a fifth is malted on the distillery's own floors and dried over peat cut on Hobbister Moor, made largely of heather; the rest is bought in already malted.
bottle.still: Distilled in copper pot stills at Kirkwall, beside the two kilns where the house dries its own malt after turning it by hand on the malting floor.

records.table: Highland Park 12 Year Old Viking Honour comes from Kirkwall on Orkney, where part of the malt is dried over island peat made of heather: honey first, then orange and fruitcake over a sweet, gentle smoke. It suits a guest who is wary of peat.
records.story: The house dates itself to 1798 and to a church beadle who, as the brand tells it, distilled on the side and hid his whisky beneath the pulpit when the excise men came. Other accounts credit a farmer who took the High Park estate above Kirkwall that year and built the distillery on the site of the smuggler's bothy, and several give 1826 as the year it first took out a licence. What sets it apart is the malt. The house turns part of its barley by hand on its own floors, about a fifth of what it needs, and dries it in two kilns over peat cut on Hobbister Moor, a few miles away. Orkney peat is made largely of heather, and its smoke is sweet and floral rather than tarry. Much of the whisky rests in dunnage warehouses with earth floors, and the house says the steady island climate takes less spirit from the casks than the mainland does. In 2017 the core range took Viking names to tell of Orkney's Norse past, and the 12 Year Old became Viking Honour, with the whisky unchanged. For a bartender it is the bottle that shows peat need not taste of tar: honey first, smoke second.

records.table: Jura 10 Year Old comes from the distillery at Craighouse on the Isle of Jura: bourbon barrels and a finish in Oloroso sherry casks give it orange, vanilla and toasted almond, with dark chocolate behind. Pour it neat or long with soda.
records.story: By the house's own account the laird of the island founded a distillery at Craighouse in 1810, at first called the Small Isles distillery, and it was licensed in 1831. James Ferguson and Sons took it over in 1876. In 1901 it closed as demand fell; the roof came off, the buildings fell into ruin, and the island lost the work the distillery had given. In 1960 a local landowner and a whisky entrepreneur set out to rebuild it, so that the island would have jobs again, and brought in a distillery designer to draw a new one on the old site. It reopened in 1963, with tall copper stills. Whyte and Mackay bought the distillery in the early 1990s, and in 2018 the range was relaunched. In August 2025 the house announced that a 12 Year Old would take the place of the 10 as its first age statement, and the 12 reached British shelves that October. Behind a bar the 10 is the gentle island malt, sweet with sherry rather than smoke, bourbon barrels first and Oloroso last.

bottle.mash: Malted barley only; the Arran malt is unpeated, and the distillery's peated spirit is bottled under its own name, Machrie Moor.
bottle.still: Distilled at Lochranza, in the north of the island, in copper pot stills; spirit first ran there on 29 June 1995.

records.table: Arran 10 Year Old is the unpeated single malt of Lochranza, in the north of the Isle of Arran, bottled at 46% ABV with no chill filtering and no added colour: citrus, honey and apple, then cinnamon and hazelnut. Pour it neat with a little water.
records.story: Arran had gone without a legal distillery for more than 150 years when a former director of Chivas Brothers set out to build one at Lochranza, in the north of the island, at a time when distilleries elsewhere were closing. Building began on 16 December 1994 and, by the house's account, was halted for a while so that a pair of golden eagles could nest in the hills above; the eagles come back most years. Spirit first ran through the stills on 29 June 1995, and the distillery was opened officially on 17 August that year. The Queen opened its visitor centre in 1997. The malt was left unpeated, and when the house began to make peated spirit it bottled it under another name, Machrie Moor. In 2019 the company opened a second distillery, at Lagg in the south of the island, and gave its single malts a new look, with the Lochranza Distillery name on the label and, as the house put it, the same whisky inside. For a bartender the 10 Year Old is the fresh, fruity island malt, bottled at 46 per cent without chill filtering, that shows an island whisky need not be smoky.

records.table: Tobermory 12 Year Old is the unpeated malt of the distillery in the harbour town of Tobermory on Mull: twelve years in American oak at 46.3% ABV, with orange, caramel, vanilla and clove. The same stills make the peated Ledaig.
records.story: The house dates itself to 1798, when a merchant of the harbour town founded a distillery on the shore at Tobermory, known for much of its life as Ledaig. Its story is one of long silences. It closed in 1837 and did not distil again until the 1870s. The Distillers Company bought it in 1916 and shut it in 1930, and it stayed silent for more than forty years. It reopened in 1972 under the Ledaig name and closed again in 1975; after more stops and starts, production resumed in 1989. The house kept the old name, Ledaig, for its heavily peated malt and Tobermory for the unpeated one. From 2017 to 2019 the distillery closed again, this time for refurbishment, and when it reopened in 2019 the 12 Year Old replaced the 10 as the unpeated malt's signature bottling, beside a new gin. For a bartender it is the lesson that peat is the house's choice, not the island's.
